Nobody's Exactly Sure How Much A Kilogram Is Right Now

Interesting vid, but it bothers me because it misrepresents the problem. Metric is based on defined physical properties, not reference standards. A kilogram is defned as the mass of one litre of water. I assume there's some caveats on temperature and pressure, but I haven't researched it. Therefore the mass of a kilogram has a defined and calcuable value. It's one the principal reasons that metric is superior; the reference can be created from the standard.

The problem being described here is creating a physical reference against which mass measurement can be calibrated. It's a small but important difference. We know exactly what a kilogram weighs. It's a problem of precision measurement, not of uncertainty.

The problem I have with metric is its precision is entirely circular.

If the value of one fundamental measurement changes, it bumps the entire system off balance. Precise, yes. Robust, no.

I think the term your looking for is interrelated. I'm can't see how it's a disadvantage; the fundamental measurements don't change.

I find it to be a significant advantage in conversion. A cubic meter of water is a 1000L and weighs 1000kg. I can easily slide back and forth between distance, volume and weight without needing to grab my calculator and a bunch of conversion tables.

So, less thinking.

That is really the only argument for the metric system's "superiority" I've heard. Less thinking.

It's not very compelling.

Both systems have served their purpose admirably. I choose the Standard system, because it makes the most sense to me.
